title: Graph Traversals, Bipartite Graphs & BFS Level Invariants

questions.prompt: In an unweighted, undirected graph, what does BFS compute from a source $s$?
options: The shortest-path (minimum edge-count) distance from $s$ to every reachable vertex.
The longest simple path from $s$.
A minimum spanning tree.
Only whether the graph is connected.
questions.explanation: BFS explores vertices in non-decreasing edge distance, so the first time a vertex is discovered is at its minimum edge-count distance. (Dijkstra handles weighted graphs; longest simple path is NP-hard.)

questions.prompt: An undirected graph has edges $1{-}2, 1{-}3, 2{-}4, 3{-}5, 4{-}6, 5{-}6$. What is the BFS distance (minimum number of edges) from vertex $1$ to vertex $6$? Enter a single integer.
questions.explanation: Layers from $1$: level 0 $\{1\}$, level 1 $\{2,3\}$, level 2 $\{4,5\}$, level 3 $\{6\}$. So $d(1,6)=3$ (e.g. path $1\to2\to4\to6$).

questions.prompt: A graph is bipartite if and only if:
options: It has no cycles.
It has no odd-length cycle.
Every vertex has even degree.
It is connected.
questions.explanation: The classic characterization: a graph is bipartite (2-colourable) iff it contains no odd cycle. A tree is bipartite; even cycles and disconnected graphs can still be bipartite.

questions.prompt: Vertices $1..8$ with edges $1{-}2, 2{-}3, 4{-}5, 6{-}7, 7{-}8, 5{-}6$. How many connected components does the graph have? Enter a single integer.
Which statements about bipartite graphs are TRUE?
options: A graph is bipartite iff it is 2-colourable.
Every tree is bipartite.
A graph containing a triangle ($K_3$) is bipartite.
A graph is bipartite iff it has no odd cycle.
questions.explanation: 2-colourability, absence of odd cycles, and bipartiteness are all equivalent. A triangle is an odd cycle of length 3, so $K_3$ is NOT bipartite (C false).

options: DFS discovers vertices in order of increasing shortest-path distance.
BFS layer order is independent of adjacency-list ordering only if the graph is a tree.
DFS uses a stack (implicitly via recursion) and BFS uses a queue.
BFS cannot detect cycles.
questions.explanation: DFS is stack/recursion-based, BFS is queue-based. DFS does NOT give increasing-distance order (A false); BFS layer *membership* is order-independent for any graph, only the within-layer order varies (B false); both BFS and DFS detect cycles (D false).

questions.prompt: Run BFS from an end vertex of a simple path graph $1{-}2{-}3{-}4{-}5{-}6$. How many distinct BFS levels (including level 0 for the source) are produced? Enter a single integer.
questions.explanation: On a path, each step advances exactly one level: levels are $\{1\},\{2\},\{3\},\{4\},\{5\},\{6\}$, i.e. $6$ levels ($0$ through $5$).

questions.prompt: During a BFS 2-colouring, you colour the source colour 0 and alternate colours along tree edges. If you ever find an edge whose endpoints share the same colour, the graph:
options: Is bipartite but not connected.
Contains an odd cycle and is therefore NOT bipartite.
Contains an even cycle.
Is a tree.
questions.explanation: A monochromatic edge after BFS colouring means there is a path of even length plus that edge, forming an odd cycle — exactly the obstruction to bipartiteness.

questions.prompt: Consider the cycle graph $1{-}2{-}3{-}4{-}5{-}1$ (a 5-cycle). What is the length of the shortest odd cycle? Enter a single integer.
questions.explanation: The only cycle is the 5-cycle itself, whose length is $5$ (odd). Shorter odd cycles (length 1 or 3) do not exist here, so the shortest odd cycle has length $5$.

questions.prompt: Which are TRUE about the BFS level invariant in an unweighted graph?
options: All edges either connect vertices in the same level, or in levels that differ by exactly 1.
No edge can connect vertices whose levels differ by 2 or more.
When a vertex $v$ at level $d+1$ is discovered, its distance is $d+1$ and cannot be improved later.
BFS may visit a vertex multiple times to find a shorter distance.
questions.explanation: BFS edges stay within a level or jump by one level (A, B); discovery distance is final (C). BFS marks vertices on discovery and never revisits them (D false).

questions.prompt: Why does plain BFS fail to find shortest paths when edges have arbitrary positive weights?
options: Because BFS cannot use a queue.
Because BFS minimizes the number of edges, not the sum of weights, so a longer path with smaller weights may be cheaper.
Because weights are always negative.
Because weighted graphs are always directed.
questions.explanation: BFS treats every edge as cost 1. With real weights, a 3-edge path of total weight 3 can beat a 1-edge path of weight 10, so BFS returns the wrong distances; Dijkstra (or 0-1 BFS for 0/1 weights) is needed.

questions.prompt: A graph has $n = 8$ vertices and $c = 2$ connected components. Any BFS or DFS forest has exactly $n - c$ tree edges. What is $n - c$? Enter a single integer.
questions.explanation: Each spanning tree of a component with $k$ vertices has $k-1$ tree edges, and the vertices sum to $n$ across $c$ components, giving $n-c$ tree edges total: $8 - 2 = 6$.

questions.prompt: To compute, for every vertex, the distance to the *nearest* of several sources, the standard trick is:
options: Run BFS once per source and take the minimum, which is optimal.
Push all sources into the queue at the start with distance 0 and run one BFS.
Sort the vertices first.
Use Dijkstra with negative edges.
questions.explanation: Multi-source BFS seeds the queue with all sources at distance 0 and runs a single BFS, giving each vertex its distance to the closest source in $O(V+E)$ — far better than one BFS per source.

questions.prompt: When implementing BFS/DFS robustly, which edge cases must be handled?
options: Self-loops (an edge from a vertex to itself) do not affect reachability but must not cause infinite loops.
Multiple edges between the same pair of vertices (multi-edges) must not break the visited check.
Disconnected graphs require restarting traversal from every unvisited vertex to cover all components.
A single isolated vertex needs a special algorithm.
questions.explanation: Self-loops, multi-edges, and disconnected graphs are the classic pitfalls (A, B, C). An isolated vertex is handled by the ordinary 'start from any unvisited vertex' loop — no special algorithm needed (D false).

questions.prompt: A recursive DFS on a path-like graph with up to $10^6$ vertices may crash. Why, and what is the fix?
options: Because of hash collisions; use a different map.
Because recursion depth can reach $10^6$, overflowing the call stack; use an explicit stack or increase the stack size.
Because integers overflow, use long long.
Because BFS uses too much memory.
questions.explanation: Deep recursion consumes one stack frame per vertex and can overflow for large $n$; replacing recursion with an explicit stack (iterative DFS) or raising the stack limit fixes it.
